topic: Return Value Optimization (RVO) and Named Return Value Optimization (NRVO)
explanation: Return Value Optimization (RVO) and its more specific variant, Named Return Value Optimization (NRVO), are compiler optimizations that significantly impact the performance and memory layout of functions returning objects.  Instead of creating a temporary object on the stack and copying it to the caller's location, the compiler directly constructs the returned object in the caller's memory location.  This avoids the overhead of constructing, copying, and destructing a temporary object. NRVO specifically applies when the returned object is assigned to a named variable.  The compiler's ability to perform RVO/NRVO depends on several factors, including the complexity of the return object's constructor, the presence of move constructors and copy constructors, and the compiler's optimization level.  Failure to perform RVO/NRVO can lead to noticeable performance degradation, particularly with large or complex objects. Understanding how and when the compiler applies RVO/NRVO is crucial for writing efficient C++ code.
code_example: MyObject(const std::string& d) : data(d) { std::cout << "MyObject constructor called\n"; }
MyObject(MyObject&& other) noexcept : data(std::move(other.data)) { std::cout << "MyObject move constructor called\n"; }
MyObject(const MyObject& other) : data(other.data) { std::cout << "MyObject copy constructor called\n"; }
example_explanation: Compile this code with different optimization levels (-O0, -O1, -O2, -O3). Observe the output.  At higher optimization levels, the compiler is *more likely* to perform NRVO, resulting in only the constructor and destructor of `MyObject` being called once, instead of the constructor, copy/move constructor, and destructor.  Without optimization, or if the compiler cannot perform RVO/NRVO (due to complex return statements or lack of move constructors, for example), the copy/move constructor and extra destructor calls will be visible. Examining the assembly code generated by the compiler will reveal whether RVO/NRVO has been applied; the absence of instructions for copying or moving the object will indicate successful optimization.  The memory layout, in the optimized case, will only involve allocation of space for the `obj` variable in `main()`, avoiding the temporary object on the stack.
